To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sensitivity of the central SWS cone pathway decreases approximately 0.1 log unit per decade of age, and that approximately half of the age-related decrease is due to a decrease in transmission of short wavelengths by the ocular lens and macular pigment.

The sensitivity of the SWS cone pathway decreases with age, with a slightly greater loss beyond age 50; the age-related loss of SWS cone sensitivity is greater than that for the other two cone pathways (MWS and LWS); there is an inverse relationship between SWS cone pathway and media transmission loss; and, after correction for media absorption, the age-related decrease of SWS cone pathway is approximately 0.08 log unit per decade, a value similar to that for LWS

the sensitivity of the short-wavelength-sensitive cone pathway decreases with age, with the greatest sensitivity loss occurring at the highest spatial frequencies, and with the greatest loss occurring at the greatest eccentricities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of age on the central visual field.
the age-related changes in visual function and the underlying anatomical substrates.
the development of new and more efficient ways to measure the sensitivity of the central visual field.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SWS cone pathway is the most susceptible pathway to age-related changes.

the age-related sensitivity decrease of the SWS cone pathway in the central visual fields was approximately 0:15 log unit per 10 years of age and was larger than the decrease of the LWS and MWS cone pathways.
the SWS cone pathway has the greatest sensitivity reduction with age, followed by the LWS cone pathway.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are two age-related changes that affect the central visual field.
age-related changes in the SWS cone pathway are greater than those in the LWS and MWS cone pathways.
the age-related loss of SWS cone function is greater than that for L- or M-cones and is related to a greater loss of media transmission for short wavelengths.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sensitivity of the SWS cone pathway declines with age.
S-cone sensitivity decreases with age and the rate of this decline is greater than that of L- and M-cone pathways.
the SWS cone pathway becomes less sensitive with aging.
